Virtual environments let each Python application keep its own isolated copy of the interpreter and packages, so different projects can require different versions of the same library without interfering with one another.

By creating a self‑contained directory tree, they resolve conflicting requirements (e.g., one app needs version 1.0 while another needs version 2.0) and ensure that upgrades in one environment do not affect others .

A namespace in Python is a mapping that associates names with objects (typically implemented as a dictionary) and it exists independently for each scope such as built‑ins, a module’s globals, or a function’s locals.
Because each module has its own private namespace, the names defined inside one module are stored separately from those in another module.
Therefore two different modules can each define a function with the same name without any conflict, since the names reside in distinct, unrelated namespaces.

When the code in the try block raises an exception that matches one of the except clauses, that except clause is executed first; after it finishes, the finally clause is run, and then execution continues after the whole try…except…finally statement (unless the finally itself overrides the flow with a return, break, etc.) .

If the exception raised in the try block does not match any of the except clauses, the finally clause is still executed, and then the original exception is re‑raised (propagated outward to an outer try or to the interpreter).

Hyper‑parameters are the settings that you pass to an estimator’s constructor and that are not learned from the data during fitting; they control how the model is built (e.g., C , kernel , gamma for an SVC or alpha for a Lasso).

In contrast, an estimator’s learned parameters are the values estimated from the training data by the fit method (such as the mean and standard deviation in a normalizer or the coefficients of a linear model).
Thus hyper‑parameters are fixed before training, while the model’s internal parameters are inferred during training.
Plain KFold, by contrast, splits the data purely by index and makes no attempt to keep class frequencies balanced across folds.
Because imbalanced data sets contain very few examples of the minority (rare) class, a non‑stratified split can easily produce a fold that has no members of that class at all.

Estimate the performance by partitioning the data into five folds, then for each fold train the estimator on the other four folds and evaluate it on the held‑out fold to obtain a performance score (e.g., accuracy).
After the five iterations, compute the average of the five scores (often also reporting the standard deviation) as the overall estimate of the model’s performance.

In scikit‑learn this is most easily done with the cross val score helper, specifying cv=5 — the function performs the five train/validation splits, returns the five scores, and you summarize them by taking their mean (and optionally their variance) .

Preprocessing steps such as StandardScaler learn scaling parameters (mean, variance) from the data they are fitted on.
If they are fitted on the whole dataset—including the test set—information from the test data leaks into the model, changing the feature space and producing overly optimistic performance estimates.

Therefore the scaler must be fit only on the training split and then the same learned transformation must be applied (via transform ) to the test data so that both sets are represented in the same way .
scikit‑learn recommends using a Pipeline (or make pipeline ) to chain the preprocessing and the estimator.

The pipeline automatically fits the transformer on the training data and applies the same transformation to any held‑out data, preventing leakage and ensuring consistent preprocessing during cross‑validation and hyper‑parameter tuning .

A virtual machine runs a complete operating system with its own kernel, hardware drivers, programs and applications, which makes it heavyweight and incurs significant overhead for each instance.

In contrast, a container is just an isolated process that includes only the files it needs and shares the host’s kernel with other containers, so many containers can run on the same underlying system with far less resource use.
Because of this, containers provide higher density and lower overhead than VMs, though they are often used together—running multiple containers inside a VM to improve utilization and reduce cost.
A container registry is the centralized service that stores and manages container images, while a repository is a specific collection of related images inside that registry.
In other words, the registry provides the overall location, and each repository groups one or more versions of a particular image within the registry .

Use a volume when you need data that the container creates or modifies to survive the container’s lifetime—i.e., you want the data to persist even after the container stops or is removed.
In contrast, bind mounts are intended for sharing specific host files or directories directly with the container.
When a container that uses a volume is deleted, the volume (and its data) remains intact; the data is not removed with the container.

In FastAPI, “dependency injection” is the mechanism by which a path‑operation function can declare the things it needs to run (its dependencies ) and FastAPI automatically creates and supplies those objects for it — it “injects” the required values instead of the developer calling the functions directly .
This approach is useful for:
Re‑using shared logic without repeating code
Enforcing security, authentication, role requirements, etc.
Handling many other cross‑cutting concerns while keeping code DRY
Declaring a separate output model (e.g., UserOut ) as the response model lets FastAPI filter the data that the endpoint actually returns.

The path‑operation function can return the full user object—including the password—but FastAPI will use the response model to omit any fields that aren’t declared in it, so the password never appears in the HTTP response.
This filtering protects sensitive information and improves security while still allowing the function to work with richer internal data.
Import HTTPException from fastapi and raise it with a 404 status code (and an optional detail) inside the path‑operation function (or any function it calls).
Raising the exception stops the rest of the path‑operation code and FastAPI automatically returns an HTTP 404 response with the provided JSON detail .

FastAPI determines the source of each function parameter by its declaration:
If the name also appears in the path template, the parameter is taken from the path .
If the parameter is a singular Python type (e.g., int , float , str , bool ), it is treated as a query parameter .
If the parameter’s type is a Pydantic model , FastAPI reads it from the request body .
For query parameters, FastAPI makes a parameter required when it is declared without a default value (e.g., needy: str ) .
It becomes optional when a default is supplied—either a concrete default (e.g., skip: int = 0 ) or None (e.g., q: str None = None ) .

Amazon S3 provides strong read‑after‑write consistency for both PUT and DELETE requests on objects in a bucket — any read that follows a successful PUT or DELETE will see the new state of the object.
The standard Init phase is limited to 10 seconds .

If the three required tasks (starting extensions, bootstrapping the runtime, and running the function’s static code) are not finished within that window, Lambda does not fail the function immediately; instead it re‑tries the Init phase when the first invocation arrives , using the function’s configured timeout as the new limit .
For functions that use provisioned concurrency, SnapStart, or Lambda Managed Instances , the 10‑second cap does not apply.
In those cases the initialization code may run for up to 15 minutes —the limit being the greater of 130 seconds or the function’s configured timeout (maximum 900 seconds) .
An IAM user is a permanent identity that represents a single person or application and has its own long‑term credentials and permissions.
An IAM role is also an identity with permissions, but it is not tied to a specific person; instead it is assumed by users, services, or federated identities to obtain temporary credentials.

A “cold start” happens when Lambda receives a request and must first create a new execution environment – downloading the function code, setting up the runtime, and running any initialization code outside the handler – before the handler can execute.
This preparation adds latency and is billed as part of the init phase .
A “warm start” occurs when a subsequent request arrives while the previously created execution environment is still retained.
Lambda reuses that already‑initialized environment, so the handler runs immediately without the extra setup time, resulting in lower latency .

It pre‑initializes execution environments so they’re ready before invocations, giving you predictable, low‑latency start times and eliminating cold‑start delays.

An Amazon S3 bucket policy is an IAM resource‑based policy—a JSON policy document that is attached directly to the bucket itself.

To let another AWS account use the bucket you must (1) add that account (or its IAM entities) as a principal in the bucket’s resource‑based policy, and (2) also provide an identity‑based policy (in the other account) that grants the principal the required S3 permissions, because the trust relationship requires both sides.
